description: Source generator that compiles .gram grammars into C# parsers.
releaseNotes: Since 0.1.0. A publication that asks only whether the input is what it says: bool TryParseR(input, out R value), one quiet reading with no message. The forms that begin where they are told: a position, a window, and both with the position moved past what was read; a reading stops where the rule ends, and reading a long text one value at a time costs the text once rather than once per value. A carrier that builds where it reads, chosen per grammar, with recovery and streaming under it. A reader over buffered input, over characters and over bytes. A yield publication stepped by the reader, one turn a MoveNext. New diagnostics, among them GRAM0009 and the report a build writes on request about carriers and the reasons for them. Two breaks to know about if you are coming from 0.1.0's positional forms: a reading that begins where it is told no longer reads the trivia after the rule, so Match.Position and Match.Length are the value's own extent and a caller that measured a value by Length reads a shorter one — a caller that only goes on from the position it was handed is unaffected; and over a grammar cut into tokens such a reading is no longer refused by a character no token begins with standing somewhere it never read, so a script with one bad character in its last line now reads the statements before it. In an editor, an edit to the class a grammar is attached to no longer compiles the grammar again unless the grammar changed, whether the grammar is a .gram file or written in the [Gram] attribute.One further break: a capture a guard can only reach through its own assignment is now handed to the `when` as the value rather than as a nullable — `T` where it was `T?` — so a condition written against the old signature with `.HasValue`, `.Value` or `.GetValueOrDefault()` no longer compiles and reads the value directly instead, and a comparison against null is reported as CS0472, the result being always true. A capture that is genuinely optional on the path is unchanged and still arrives nullable. Fixed: a `when` over a repeated text capture whose body holds anything else — `(y: D & ','?){2}` over "1,2" — was handed only the last turn rather than the turns joined, so a guard could refuse what the rule would have built, or accept what it should have refused; a `switch` selector over the same kind of capture had the same defect and is fixed with it. Fixed, and present since 0.1.0: a reading that gave back an alternative could leave a record pointing at one it had rolled back. On a thread whose first parse met it, the parse threw IndexOutOfRangeException; on a thread an earlier, larger parse had warmed, it went on without saying so. Every input found to reach it was one the grammar refuses, and the refusal it returned was the right one; no accepted input was found to reach it, over the tests of every grammar here and some 7,700 statements of real T-SQL. A parser has to be generated again to get the fix. Fixed: a capture over a lookahead inside a repetition, such as `(y: ?=D & D & ','?){2}`, now joins its pieces instead of keeping only the last one, so a guard and the built value agree. Where a lookahead's pieces overlap, the join now asks each pair of neighbours whether they meet, instead of summing lengths that could cancel the overlap out. Fixed, in a left-recursive (fold) rule: a step's guard and construction now get the step's own captures, not an earlier step's or the base's. A value repeated inside a step is now the step's array, not its last piece. An absent optional inside a step now reaches the guard and the construction as null, not as the base's piece or an empty string. Two compile errors in the emitted code, CS1503 and CS0103, are gone. New refusal: GRAM4007 now refuses a fold step that collects a value another alternative holds once — a behaviour change, since such a grammar used to compile and silently hand the step only the last value it collected. In an editor, a grammar written inline in a `[Gram("…")]` attribute is no longer compiled again for an edit anywhere else in its host file — moving or editing unrelated code above or below the attribute used to recompile it too; only an edit to the grammar's own text does now, as a `.gram` file grammar already worked. An external `@Name` is now found by asking the compilation for that name directly rather than by scanning and testing every name it declares, which made re-checking a grammar after a host-only edit faster. Fixed: a guard's shortcut for finding the record it stands in could read a record a give-back had already discarded and build the wrong kind of value into it, which could throw IndexOutOfRangeException or NullReferenceException in a generated parser on some refused input, or rarely use the wrong value where nothing threw; no accepted input was found to reach it. In a left-recursive (fold) rule on the immediate carrier, a step given back after it had itself read a value of the rule's own type could leave that abandoned value standing in place of the fold's value so far, changing an accepted result. A step's construction — the code built for `=>` — now sees the text of its own application, from where the fold began to where that step ended, rather than the whole call's text, wherever it asks for `parserText`, `parserSpan` or its location. New diagnostic GRAM4031: a guard in a fold step that names another step's captured name for the value so far, which this step has none of, is refused at generation time instead of being left as a name unbound anywhere in the emitted guard method. The C# the generator writes into your compilation — the parser and the support code it copies there — may now be used, modified and distributed under terms of your choice, without carrying the MIT notice; see the end of LICENSE and the package README. Fixed: a literal that ignores case ('s'i) after a lookahead for the same letters could make the generated reader refuse text the grammar accepts ("aS" after (?!'s' & any)+); and a run that a padded separator such as ' '* & '|' & ' '* ends no longer costs the square of the padding in the generated reader, as it already did not in the engine. Recovering past a field nothing recognizes had the same shape and cost: it searched again from every character of the run's padding for where it might end, and now scans ahead the same way reading does. A run followed by more of the same optional padding before its own stop, as in `Text & ' '* & ('|' & ' '* | eof)`, is now proved, wherever nothing in the grammar could ask for a shorter reading there, never to need to give characters back either, so it too reads in one pass instead of a turn at a time. A run bounded by a small set of stop characters — this scan among them — is found by searching for them directly, and that search took only a stop literal's written casing where the literal ignores case, so it could run past what the literal folds to as well ('s'i also reads U+017F, 'μ'i reads U+00B5), reading text into a value the stop should have ended, or refusing text the grammar accepts; the search now falls back to the ordinary matcher for such a literal. Fixed: a guard's `when` condition was handed every capture whose name merely appeared inside its C# text, not only the ones the condition actually names — a guard that only wrote `context` was also handed a capture named `c`, one that only wrote `parserSpan` was also handed `p` — which could throw building a value nothing asked for. A capture named for a C# keyword had the opposite failure: the same search never matches the escaped parameter it becomes (`@class` for `class`), so naming it in a guard lost it to a compile error or a silent read of an unrelated same-named member in scope. Both are fixed by asking only for the names a condition's own C# actually contains.
